nameStory: The red-bellied snake gets its name from the most obvious feature that catches your eye when you spot one - its bright reddish-orange belly that contrasts beautifully with its brown back. When these little snakes feel threatened, they sometimes flip over to show off that colorful underside, almost like they're saying 'Look at my pretty belly!' It's nature's way of giving this humble snake a memorable calling card.
description: The red-bellied snake is one of New England's smallest and most secretive serpents, typically measuring just 8-12 inches long - about the length of a ruler. These slender snakes have brown or grayish backs that help them blend into leaf litter, but their claim to fame is their vibrant reddish-orange belly that gives them their name. They're completely harmless members of the colubrid family, spending most of their time hidden under logs, rocks, or decomposing leaves. Despite their shy nature, they're actually quite common throughout New England, though you're more likely to find one by accident than by searching.

idTips.label: Belly Color
idTips.description: The bright reddish-orange to coral-pink belly is the most reliable identification feature - it feels smooth to the touch and the color is consistent from chin to tail

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Exceptionally small and slender, typically 8-12 inches long and about as thick as a pencil - feels delicate and lightweight if handled

idTips.label: Pattern
idTips.description: Back ranges from brown to gray with sometimes a faint light stripe down the spine - the scales feel smooth and have a subtle sheen in sunlight

idTips.label: Head Shape
idTips.description: Small, narrow head that's barely wider than the neck with tiny dark eyes - typical of harmless snakes with a gentle, non-threatening appearance

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Extremely secretive and may curl into a tight ball when threatened, sometimes exposing the bright belly as a defensive display

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found under cover objects in moist areas - if you smell rich, earthy decomposition and feel damp soil, you're in prime red-bellied snake territory

habitat: Red-bellied snakes prefer moist, wooded areas throughout New England where they can stay hidden under logs, rocks, leaf litter, and decomposing vegetation. You'll often find them in mixed hardwood forests, woodland edges, and even suburban areas with sufficient ground cover. They particularly favor spots with rich, dark soil that stays damp, often near streams or in areas where organic matter accumulates.

seasonality.spring: Emerges from winter hiding spots in April and May, often found under sun-warmed rocks or logs as they become active. This is when they're most likely to be discovered during yard cleanup activities.
seasonality.summer: Most active during warm, humid evenings and can sometimes be found in the open on rainy nights. During hot days, they retreat deep under cover objects where the soil stays cool and moist.
seasonality.fall: Feeding heavily before winter, they're occasionally spotted during the day under cover objects. Late fall is when they begin seeking deeper winter shelters under rock piles or in rotting logs.
seasonality.winter: Dormant underground or deep in rotting logs and rock crevices below the frost line, entering a state called brumation until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Red-bellied snakes are specialized slug and earthworm hunters with tiny teeth perfectly designed for gripping slimy prey - they can actually extract a snail from its shell by grabbing it and spinning their body like a corkscrew!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with DeKay's brownsnake, but the red-bellied snake's bright orange-red belly is unmistakable compared to the brownsnake's pale pink or yellowish belly. Memory trick: 'Red-belly' has the word red right in the name, and that bright belly color is exactly what you'll see!
compareHints: The red-bellied snake is easily distinguished from its close relative, DeKay's brownsnake, by its much brighter red-orange belly color versus the brownsnake's pale pink or cream belly. Red-bellied snakes are also typically smaller and more slender than DeKay's brownsnakes. Both species share similar secretive habits and woodland preferences, but the belly color is a dead giveaway once you flip them over for a look.

relatedSpecies.distinction: DeKay's Brownsnake differs from its cousin the Red-bellied Snake by having spots instead of stripes and lacking the distinctive bright red or orange belly coloration.
